title: What not to put on the site for a law practice
metaTitle: Law practice website mistakes worth cutting
excerpt: Cut marble, Latin, and vague excellence from a law firm site. Keep the matters you take and a clear way to request a consultation.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it, a plain working desk rather than a costume.
caption: A desk set up for the work, with the extra screens in the background. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a law firm remove from its website?
faqs.answer: Remove marble, Latin, stock gavels, and lines like premier or full service that any firm could use. Remove practice-area grids that have no outcome or boundary, and remove faces that are not your staff. Keep the matters you take and a way to request a consultation.

faqs.question: Is a longer law firm website better?
faqs.answer: Not by length. Google's helpful-content guidance says Google does not have a preferred word count. A short site that names the matter, the person, and the next step is easier to keep true. Thin suburb pages and unnamed blog posts add volume without helping a client who has a deadline.

faqs.question: What is a mistake to leave on the contact page?
faqs.answer: A ten-field form, a chat tool dressed up as a lawyer, and a phone number nobody answers. Ask for the matter, the deadline, and a way to reply. Say how fast a person actually responds, and say that the first reply is not legal advice.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The most common law practice website mistakes are costume and volume. Cut the marble texture and the Latin. They reassure the people inside the firm and confuse a client who is choosing counsel under time pressure. Keep the kind of matter you take, and keep a clear way to request a consultation. A shorter site that tells the truth will do more for that client than a long site that performs taste.

Google's helpful-content guidance is direct about length. It asks whether you are writing to a word count because you heard that Google prefers one, and it answers that Google does not. The same guidance treats trust as the important part of experience and expertise on topics that can affect safety or finances. A legal site sits in that group. Extra pages that repeat a mood do not create trust. Nielsen Norman Group found that people read only about a quarter of the text on pages they open, and often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. Whatever you keep has to survive that skim.

## What to take off the page

Start with a cut list you can apply this week. If an element does not help a client name the matter or request a consultation, it is a candidate.

Marble, columns, scales, gavels, and a Latin motto. These are the costume. They photograph as "law" and communicate nothing about leases, letters, or owner disputes. A real room and a real sentence replace them.

Lines any firm could paste on. Premier. Esteemed. Full service. Committed to excellence. Solutions-oriented. Bespoke. They soothe a partner reading the draft. They give a client with a Friday deadline nothing to sort on.

A grid of every matter the firm has ever touched, each with the same two sentences. If you cannot write an outcome and a boundary, the item is not ready to be a service. Move it off, or write it properly.

Awards and rankings as the first screen. A current, true badge can sit low. It cannot be the argument. A client cannot hire a badge to read a lease.

Stock handshakes, skylines, and diverse teams that are not your team. If the face is not someone who works there, do not put it on the about page. Absence is more honest than a rented smile.

A chat widget that implies a lawyer is typing. If the person on the other end cannot give advice, do not dress the tool up as counsel. A button that requests a consultation is plainer and safer.

## Why the costume survives the review

The marble stays because the internal audience is anxious. Partners want the site to look like the firms they respect, and those firms bought the same texture. The review happens on a laptop in a meeting, where Latin looks like tradition and a long page looks like substance.

The client is not in that meeting. They are sorting three sites between other work, often on a phone. Tradition that they cannot read is noise. Substance they cannot match to their letter is noise. The internal sigh of relief is not a usability test.

There is a second reason the cuts get reversed. Someone adds a paragraph so the page does not look empty. Emptiness, in the first screen, is often the matter finally being visible. Fill the space with the consultation and the boundary, not with a second motto.

A third reason is search folklore. A vendor offers a page for every suburb and every synonym of lawyer. Google's people-first questions warn against content made mainly to attract search, and against entering topics without real depth. Twenty thin location pages are that pattern. One page that says where you practice, and which matters you take there, is the version a client can use. It is also the version you can keep accurate.

## What stays, and in what words

Keep the kind of matter in the client's language, near the top of the homepage and on each service. Shop leases for independent tenants. Employment letters for small companies. Owner agreements before someone wires money. Add the boundary in the same breath. Who it is for. Who it is not for. Which jurisdictions.

Keep the consultation, labeled the same way everywhere, with what happens after they send it, how fast you really reply, and what to have ready. A short form. A named role that reads it. A sentence that the first reply is not legal advice.

Keep the people who do the work, with the matters they handle. Keep one proof page only when you can show a constraint and a decision without identifying a client or inventing a quote. Keep the fee shape if clients always ask, even when the dollar figure varies.

Keep the address, the hours, and a phone number only if a person answers in the way the page describes. A dead number is a mistake, not a courtesy.

That set is a whole site. Homepage, services, people, proof if you have it, pricing if you can say the shape, and contact. You can add a note on how conflicts work. You do not need a library of posts to look alive.

## Mistakes that look like content

Some additions are not marble, and they still waste the client.

A blog with no owner, posted so the site looks current. If you write, write for the client who has the letter, and put the author's name on it. Google asks who created the content, and a nameless post fails that question. If you will not maintain it, do not start it.

Doorway pages that swap the suburb and keep the paragraph. They are hard to tell apart, and Google's title-link guidance warns that boilerplate titles and inaccurate titles get rewritten or ignored. Write one clear page instead of thirty echoes.

A downloadable brochure that repeats the site in worse type. If the PDF is the real sales pitch, the site is a lobby. Put the pitch on the page, where it can be updated without emailing a file.

Fake quotations from grateful clients. You do not get to write the sentence and sign their industry. If you lack permission, skip the quote. The decision on a proof page is stronger than a compliment you authored.

A promise about outcomes. Win rates, "we always settle," "no fee unless we win," unless every word is true, permitted where you practice, and still true next month. A careless superlative is a mistake that outlives the redesign.

Keyword lines in the footer. "Lawyer lawyer lawyer" in a city list is not a service. It is a confession that the headings were unclear. Fix the headings.

## A shorter site is a maintained site

Every block you keep has to be updated when a lawyer leaves, a fee shape changes, or you stop taking a matter. Short sites get updated. Long sites grow a page that still offers a consultation with someone who is gone.

Give one person the job of the cut. Not a committee. The committee will restore "excellence" because removing it feels rude. The standard is the client with a deadline. Read each block and ask what decision it changes. If the answer is none, cut it.

Google's note that there is no preferred word count is permission to stop padding. It is not permission to be vague. The remaining sentences should be more specific, not fewer and foggier. "We help businesses" is short and useless. "We review shop leases for independent tenants in Victoria" is short and usable.

When you are unsure, cut the adjective and keep the noun. Keep lease, letter, deadline, name, consultation. Release premier, bespoke, and esteemed. The page will sound more like a firm that does the work, which is the tone formality was reaching for.

## How to review the cuts

Print the homepage, or just view it on a phone, and mark anything that is costume. Then mark anything a stranger could not act on. What remains should be the matter, the boundary, the person, and the ask.

Show that screen to someone who is not a lawyer for ten seconds. Ask what the firm takes and how they would request time. If they mention the marble, you did not cut enough. If they name the matter, you can stop adding sections.

Check the search result titles after the next crawl, or at least the title element you control. Each page should name its job. "Shop lease reviews" beats "Practice areas | Excellence." Distinct titles are a basic part of Google's title-link advice, and they are also how a client tells two of your pages apart in a hurry.

Look at the contact form last. Cuts elsewhere do not help if the ask is still ten fields and a captcha. The consultation is the point of the shorter site. Make it the easiest true thing on the page.

## What not to cut

Do not cut the boundary in the name of sounding welcoming. A false welcome creates the wrong consultation. Do not cut the sentence that says the first reply is not legal advice. Do not cut jurisdiction. Do not cut the name of the person who actually does the work in order to look more institutional.

Do not cut accessibility because the marble was doing the contrast work. If you remove a dark photograph, reset the type so it still meets a readable contrast on the plain background. W3C's WCAG overview is the standard to keep in mind: the page still has to be perceivable and operable. A beautiful cut that leaves gray text on a pale field is a new mistake.

Do not cut the truth about speed. If you reply the next business day, say that, even if it sounds less fierce than "instant."

After a law site tells the truth, it is worth seeing the same standard in a neighboring profession, where the buyer is a founder who wants a calm expert rather than a client with a hearing date. Read [what an accounting firm homepage has to prove](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-an-accounting-firm). The proof there is who does the work and for whom, and the costume to refuse is a skyline and the word excellence.

When you want a cut list applied with the same bluntness to a marketing site, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The sites that hold up are the ones that stayed specific.
